$comment: Catalog-level UI builder policy for :catalog, beside its cover sheet. PER-COMPONENT policy is NOT here — it is @BuilderComponent beside @CatalogComponent on the sticker, so a component is never renamed in two places; this file carries only what belongs to no component. The knowledge it moves used to live in Kotlin inside the preview server (ProductionUiBuilderRuntime.wearM3Catalog, UiBuilderRenderer's Wear constants), which meant a fourth catalog cost a release of a repository that has never seen this one's components. The contract: https://github.com/yschimke/compose-preview-server/blob/main/docs/design/UI_BUILDER_CATALOG_CONTRACT.md — what this repository owes it: https://github.com/yschimke/compose-ai-tools/blob/main/docs/design/UI_BUILDER_CATALOG_POLICY.md. Nothing reads this file yet: it is authored so it can be proved equivalent to what the server synthesises today, BEFORE the server changes a reader.
$comment_catalogId: The one place this catalog's two names show. The delivery system is `wear-m3-catalog` (catalog.spec.json), but the builder — and every design ever saved against it — has known this catalog as `wear-m3`, and a design document stores that string in every node. So the builder id is declared rather than defaulted from `system`. It is also why the server's `--ui-builder-native-catalog wear-m3=wear-m3-catalog` mapping cannot go away with the rest of that flag: the contract's 'a builder catalog is a served catalog' holds by construction for the sibling :remote-catalog, whose system IS `remote-m3`, and by declaration here.

wasm.reason: The canvas draws this catalog's components with a Compose Multiplatform build of Wear Compose — the Android AAR has no browser variant — so each is the component itself rather than an impression of it. What is still the canvas's own: the screen frame (the extent has no viewport for a real scaffold), the unrolled list (a long screenshot turns the row transformation off), and the type scale, which is the mobile theme's. Author on it; check a size on the Android preview, which compiles this design's own generated Kotlin against the real AAR.

native.reason: The generated Kotlin compiled against this module's own classpath and rendered under Robolectric: the same lane that produces this catalog's stickers.

frame.$comment_seedDevice: The first entry of catalog.spec.json's breakpoints table, named explicitly rather than defaulted: a new design opening at a size this catalog does not document would be drawn against padding nobody measured.

geometry.$comment: WRITTEN BY A TEST, NEVER BY HAND. catalog/src/test/kotlin/ee/schimke/wearm3catalog/ScreenScaffoldContentPaddingTest.kt composes the real ScreenScaffold over a real TransformingLazyColumn at each round size, reads the padding Wear Compose computes, and asserts this block equals its measurement. Editing these numbers is a failing test, which is the entire reason the block lives in this repository: the preview server carried a transcribed copy, and a number copied out of a render goes stale silently. ONLY WHAT THAT PROBE MEASURES IS HERE. The frame's corner radius, its sampled colours and its clock geometry are still constants in the server's renderer, sampled from this catalog's stitched capture; they move here when a probe measures them, and until then this catalog does not claim numbers it has not taken.

$comment_builtins: The only components this file may declare, and the reason the restriction exists: a builtin has no call site, so it cannot be in the component record and there is no sticker to annotate. Each names the structural role that writes it. Everything else this catalog offers a builder comes from the record, with @BuilderComponent on the sticker for whatever the signature cannot say.

properties.name: timeText
properties.notes: The curved status strip's text. Frozen rather than live, so a design's render does not change every minute.

properties.name: scrollIndicator
properties.notes: Whether the generated screen gives `ScreenScaffold` a scroll indicator.

properties.name: background
properties.notes: The screen's background; Wear Material 3's `background` when absent.

properties.name: verticalSpacingDp
properties.notes: `Arrangement.spacedBy` between items; 4dp is the Wear list default.

colorTokens.$comment: The theme roles a colour property or a background modifier may name — the vocabulary, not the values. A Wear design resolves these against Wear Material 3's own scheme, which is why the sampled colours the canvas draws the frame with are a separate question and still live in the server's renderer until a probe here measures them. The list itself is Material 3's, which Wear Material 3 shares: a design that names `onSurfaceVariant` means the same role on both, and on a watch it happens to be a warm #FFDCC2 rather than the grey a phone puts there.

menu.$comment: This catalog's own @file:CatalogGroup(section = …) vocabulary, ordered as a person reaches for it rather than alphabetically. A group a component names that this list omits sorts after the ones it lists, so adding a section in code does not make its components vanish from the panel. THAT FALLBACK WAS DOING ALL THE WORK: this list used to name Layout, Navigation, Actions, Selection, Containment, Communication, Motion, Styles and Horologist — a vocabulary the stickers stopped using — so 72 of 76 components landed in groups it did not name and the builder alphabetised them after nine EMPTY shelves. The order now names the groups the components actually carry; `ui-builder-equivalence.sh` is what re-checks that, and remote-m3 has a test for it (`the menu order covers the groups the shelf actually uses`) that this catalog still lacks.

$comment_code: No `code` block yet, so the export stays `record`: a call site printed per node from the component record. The structural half of a Wear screen — ScreenScaffold's scroll state having to be the same object the TransformingLazyColumn inside it holds, SurfaceTransformation only being writable inside `item { }`, a dialog being a sibling of the scaffold rather than a child — is what the templates are for, and they arrive with the template engine rather than ahead of it. Templates declared before anything can run them would publish structure nobody has compiled, which is the one thing this contract is meant to stop.
$comment_templates: The two designs a new `wear-m3` design can start from, as branch-relative paths. Both are this repository's own documents under `ui-builder/designs/`, transcribed from the seed builders in compose-ui-builder (`wearScreenUiBuilderDocument` / `blankWearScreenUiBuilderDocument`) and authored here from then on — this file and the documents are the source of truth for what a new design opens as, so a template edit is a change to this repository rather than a release of the builder. The design-artifacts pipeline copies `ui-builder/designs/` to the delivery branch beside this generated file — see `catalog-ui-builder.mjs`, which reports a path the bundle does not carry rather than publishing a chooser entry that 404s. `wear-screen` leads because a blank starting point comes before the worked sample, and the sample is `wear-list`: THIS catalog's own activity list, row for row. The entry is a bare path today because that is the only shape the schema accepts; the label and supporting text the New design chooser prints (`Wear screen` / `Activity list`) still live in the builder's Kotlin, and the object form that carries them lands with the reader that consumes it (UI_BUILDER_SEED_TEMPLATES.md step 3). What this repository owes in return is the round trip the preview server cannot run: the generated Kotlin names `AppScaffold`, `ScreenScaffold` and `rememberTransformationSpec`, so only this module can compile it — see WearScreenTemplateRoundTripTest.
$comment_components: Shelves stated here rather than derived. A component's group comes from the sticker that draws it, and where ONE symbol is drawn by many stickers the generator takes the alphabetically-first one — so `Text`, drawn by 39 stickers, was shelved under `AlertDialog`'s group and appeared on Dialogs. Stating the group is the sanctioned per-component fix; the alternative is a heuristic nobody can predict. Only the components whose derived shelf is WRONG are listed: `Button` and `Card` are derived from a collision too and happen to land correctly, and deriving a right answer is not a reason to restate it here.

wear-m3/text.$comment: 39 stickers draw Text; the first alphabetically is AlertDialog, so it shelved on Dialogs. The builder properties `Text`'s signature cannot state; the call-site ones (`text`, `color`, `fontSizeSp`, `textAlign`, …) are still derived from the record.

propertyCapabilities.name: style
propertyCapabilities.notes: The role the text is set in, resolved against Wear's own type scale.

propertyCapabilities.name: alignment
propertyCapabilities.notes: Where the text sits in a parent that gives it more room than it needs.

propertyCapabilities.name: weight
propertyCapabilities.notes: The share of a parent's remaining space the text takes.

wear-m3/icon.$comment: 22 stickers draw Icon; same AlertDialog collision, same wrong shelf.

wear-m3/list-header.$comment: 4 stickers; first is FastScrollingTransformingLazyColumn, which is where it went. `ListHeader` takes a content lambda, so its record derives a `content` slot and no `text`, and every Wear template (whose first row is a header) was refused with `UNKNOWN_PROPERTY: property text is not declared by wear-m3/list-header`. Stated as a label leaf, the vocabulary `WearCanvasAdapters` reads: `text`, `maxLines`, `overflow`.

propertyCapabilities.name: maxLines
propertyCapabilities.notes: How many lines the label may occupy before it truncates.

propertyCapabilities.name: overflow
propertyCapabilities.notes: What a truncated label does at its edge.

wear-m3/list-sub-header.$comment: The same label leaf as `list-header`, for the same reason: the record derives `icon` and `label` slots, and the canvas adapter reads `text`, `maxLines` and `overflow`.

propertyCapabilities.name: maxLines
propertyCapabilities.notes: How many lines the label may occupy before it truncates.

propertyCapabilities.name: overflow
propertyCapabilities.notes: What a truncated label does at its edge.

wear-m3/screen-scaffold.excluded: the `wear-m3/screen-scaffold` builtin above is the screen root, and this record derives the same id. Left in, the record wins the id and the builtin is dropped: the screen composes as a Container with ScreenScaffold's lambda parameters as slots (`timeText`, `scrollIndicator`) and none of the builder's properties, so every Wear template is refused on creation. The Wear screen exporter writes `ScreenScaffold` without a record.

wear-m3/card.$comment: `variant` picks which of Wear's four card composables is written, and `stableKey` is the lazy list's `key`; neither is a parameter of `Card`, so the record cannot derive them. `shape` and the rest are still derived.

propertyCapabilities.name: stableKey
propertyCapabilities.notes: The item's identity, written as the generated lazy list's `key`.

wear-m3/app-scaffold.$comment: The same first-sticker-alphabetically collision as the four above, reached one level further down: no sticker calls `AppScaffold` directly on this shelf at all. `ScreenSticker` (CatalogTheme.kt) is the frame that supplies it, `FastScrollingList` is the alphabetically-first sticker drawn in one, and `sections/FastScrolling.kt` — which names neither symbol — is what carries the `@file:CatalogGroup`. So the Wear app frame published under Horologist, next to a fast-scrolling demo (#491). `Lists and screens` is where it belongs: it is the app half of the `screen-scaffold` pair the builtin above already shelves there, and `sections/Lists.kt` is the file whose stickers are about screens.

wear-m3/time-text.$comment: Rode the same indirection as `app-scaffold` above and for the same reason — `ScreenSticker` draws the clock inside its `AppScaffold`, and that sticker's file decided the shelf for both. `Text` is where the catalog itself declares it: `@CatalogComponent(id = "TimeText")` is in `sections/TextComponents.kt`, whose group is `Text`, beside `animated-text` and `fading-expanding-label`.

wear-m3/circular-progress-indicator.$comment: Same first-sticker-alphabetically collision as the three above. LoadingButton in sections/Buttons.kt draws a bare CircularProgressIndicator inside the Button/Loading sticker, and it sorts ahead of the ProgressIndicators.kt stickers, so the shelf came out Buttons — next to `button` and `child-button`, and away from arc-, linear- and segmented-circular-, which are the other three rings. ProgressIndicators.kt is where @CatalogComponent(id = "CircularProgressIndicator") actually declares it.

wear-m3/edge-button.$comment: The same collision, but it bound the WRONG OVERLOAD as well as the wrong shelf, which is why this entry pins `record` and not just `group`. Two EdgeButtons are published: AlertDialogDefaults.EdgeButton, the one the dialog owns, and EdgeButtonKt.EdgeButton, the standalone component EdgeButtons.kt declares. AlertDialog sorts first, so `wear-m3/edge-button` resolved to the dialog's overload and shelved on Dialogs, leaving the standalone EdgeButton reachable under no id at all. Naming the record here rebinds the id to the component the catalog means by it and returns it to its own shelf.

wear-m3/sticker.excluded: the catalog's own preview frame, not a Wear Material 3 component: every sticker is drawn inside one, the Design Kit publishes no node for it, and nobody places one in a design. Same exclusion, and the same reason, as `m3/sticker` in the sibling m3-catalog. The bare frame — `CatalogMaterialTheme { Box { content() } }`. Published on `Text`.

wear-m3/screen-sticker.excluded: the catalog's own preview frame, not a Wear Material 3 component: every sticker is drawn inside one, the Design Kit publishes no node for it, and nobody places one in a design. Same exclusion, and the same reason, as `m3/sticker` in the sibling m3-catalog. The same frame inside an `AppScaffold` with a stubbed `TimeText`, so a sticker draws as a screen. Published on `Fast scrolling`.

wear-m3/transparent-screen-sticker.excluded: the catalog's own preview frame, not a Wear Material 3 component: every sticker is drawn inside one, the Design Kit publishes no node for it, and nobody places one in a design. Same exclusion, and the same reason, as `m3/sticker` in the sibling m3-catalog. The screen frame without a background fill. Published on `Progress indicators`.

wear-m3/full-screen-sticker.excluded: the catalog's own preview frame, not a Wear Material 3 component: every sticker is drawn inside one, the Design Kit publishes no node for it, and nobody places one in a design. Same exclusion, and the same reason, as `m3/sticker` in the sibling m3-catalog. The screen frame with the theme background filled. Published on `Sign-in`.

wear-m3/edge-button-sticker.excluded: the catalog's own preview frame, not a Wear Material 3 component: every sticker is drawn inside one, the Design Kit publishes no node for it, and nobody places one in a design. Same exclusion, and the same reason, as `m3/sticker` in the sibling m3-catalog. The frame pinned to the 192dp base screen width, so an edge button draws at the width whose arc it is clipped to. Published on `Edge-hugging buttons`.

wear-m3/animated-sticker.excluded: the catalog's own preview frame, not a Wear Material 3 component: every sticker is drawn inside one, the Design Kit publishes no node for it, and nobody places one in a design. Same exclusion, and the same reason, as `m3/sticker` in the sibling m3-catalog. The frame for a motion recording — an `AppScaffold` with the clock stubbed out. Already absent from the component menu, so this entry changes nothing there; it is here to put the published reason on the record, which keeps every excluded component and carries the `excluded` string beside it.

wear-m3/edge-button-screen.excluded: the catalog's own preview frame, not a Wear Material 3 component: every sticker is drawn inside one, the Design Kit publishes no node for it, and nobody places one in a design. Same exclusion, and the same reason, as `m3/sticker` in the sibling m3-catalog. The scrollable screen the edge-button reveal is recorded through. Its own KDoc says it is not a component frame: the kit publishes no screen cell for it. Already absent from the component menu, so this entry changes nothing there; it is here to put the published reason on the record, which keeps every excluded component and carries the `excluded` string beside it.

wear-m3/wear-screen.excluded: the catalog's own preview frame, not a Wear Material 3 component: every sticker is drawn inside one, the Design Kit publishes no node for it, and nobody places one in a design. Same exclusion, and the same reason, as `m3/sticker` in the sibling m3-catalog. The list sections' screen frame — `MaterialTheme` plus an `AppScaffold` with a stubbed `TimeText`. It sits in a file that carries a `@file:CatalogGroup`, which is the only reason it published on a plausible-looking shelf (`Lists and screens`) rather than a scattered one.

wear-m3/media-row-sticker.excluded: the catalog's own preview frame, not a Wear Material 3 component: every sticker is drawn inside one, the Design Kit publishes no node for it, and nobody places one in a design. Same exclusion, and the same reason, as `m3/sticker` in the sibling m3-catalog. The Media Controls row frame — a `Sticker` narrowed to the kit's 192dp base screen width and a fixed row height. Same as `wear-screen`: its file's `@file:CatalogGroup` is why it published on `Media controls` rather than a scattered shelf.
